title: Sale of Nigeria's state power company (NEPA/PHCN)
point: Abuja, where the Bureau of Public Enterprises ran the sale and the Abuja distribution company was handed over (national measure)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its Privatization Support Project (IDA credit, US$114.29 million, 2001) paid advisers to break up NEPA into separate companies, design the power market and tariff rules, and run the sale of the generation and distribution companies. The World Bank says the 2010 power strategy carried out the privatization plan developed with this project's support.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Under the 2005-2007 Policy Support Instrument, Nigeria listed among outstanding benchmarks the bid opening for concessioning the Transmission Company of Nigeria before the final IMF Board review (letter of intent, September 2007).

conditions: World Bank Privatization Support Project components: corporate restructuring of NEPA, 'privatization of entities formed from NEPA', and a tariff strategy (World Bank completion report, 2011). IMF Policy Support Instrument: the government committed to complete 'bid opening for concessioning of Transmission Company of Nigeria' before the final IMF Board review (Nigeria letter of intent, 26 September 2007).

companies.name: KANN Consortium
companies.role: Took over the Abuja Electricity Distribution Company in November 2013 (Daily Trust).

companies.name: Manitoba Hydro International
companies.role: Given management control of the Transmission Company of Nigeria (Daily Trust).

community: On 1 November 2013 ten distribution and four generation companies passed to private owners. Daily Trust reported that new owners disengaged staff at most plants. The electricity workers' union NUEE said more than 50,000 former PHCN staff were still owed entitlements and over 5,000 had received nothing (Guardian Nigeria). In 2019 the union said over 2,000 disengaged staff had not been paid since 2013, that the new distribution companies paid some workers half salaries, and that some did not pass on pension deductions (TheCable). A new tariff order (MYTO 2) in June 2013 raised bills (Daily Trust).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: The union struck in early October 2013 over unpaid severance; an agreement to pay by end-November was signed. In December 2019 the union struck again over unpaid benefits, causing hours of blackouts, and called it off within 24 hours after government intervention (TheCable). Transmission stayed in state hands under a management contract.

sources.title: Nigeria - Privatization Support Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report
Nigeria: Letter of Intent (Policy Support Instrument)
2013: a year of privatised power sector
Unpaid benefits, half salaries… demands of electricity union workers who went on strike
Govt owes 50,000 ex-workers of PHCN – NUEE

confidence_note: The World Bank's own report describes funding the break-up and sale. The worker figures come from the union; the government did not publish a count of jobs lost.

title: Sale of Eleme Petrochemicals
point: Eleme petrochemical plant near Port Harcourt (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Lists the Eleme sale (US$225 million, 11.9% of all proceeds) among privatizations achieved under its Privatization Support Project. Its private arm, the IFC, lent US$75 million and mobilised US$80 million for the buyer (Bretton Woods Project).

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The Bretton Woods Project says the sale was listed as a structural reform under the IMF Policy Support Instrument in October 2005.

conditions: World Bank Privatization Support Project (2001-2010) financed the privatization programme that sold Eleme (World Bank completion report, 2011). The IMF Policy Support Instrument's reform list included sales of state assets (Bretton Woods Project, 2008).

companies.name: Indorama Group
companies.role: Buyer; reportedly received a 75% stake against a memorandum that set a 51/49 split (Bretton Woods Project).
companies.hq: Indonesia (as stated by Bretton Woods Project)

community: The National Union of Petroleum and Natural Gas Workers (NUPENG) said the plant was undervalued. The Bretton Woods Project reports that staff fell from 1,000 to 296 after the sale.
suppression: The Bretton Woods Project reports that troops took the plant by force for the handover.
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: Indorama ran the plant. A House of Representatives investigation of privatizations followed in March 2008 (Bretton Woods Project).

sources.title: Nigeria - Privatization Support Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report
Facilitating whose power? WB and IMF policy influence in Nigeria's energy sector

confidence_note: The World Bank documents that the sale was part of its project. The job-loss figure, the use of troops and the IMF benchmark listing come from one advocacy source citing the union, not from the IMF or the buyer.

title: Sale of Ghana's state gold mines at Tarkwa
point: Tarkwa gold mine, Wassa West District (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its Mining Sector Rehabilitation Project (IDA credit 1921, 1988) paid to restructure the State Gold Mining Corporation (SGMC) and to attract buyers. The World Bank says the credit helped bring about the sale of SGMC's three mines, including Tarkwa. It also funded the start of the 1986 Minerals and Mining Law.

conditions: Under the Mining Sector Rehabilitation Project, the government and lenders agreed to fund the work needed to attract investors and sell all of SGMC's mines, with cost cutting and downsizing at SGMC (World Bank completion report, 1997).

companies.name: Gold Fields
companies.role: Took over the Tarkwa mine in July 1993 and later converted it to surface mining.

community: Earthworks reports that mining displaced 30,000 people in the Wassa area between 1990 and 1998 (it does not say who counted). It says land was taken from farmers 'often using force and without adequate compensation'. On 16 October 2001 a cyanide spill at Gold Fields' Tarkwa mine left more than 1,000 people without drinking water and affected at least five villages. Researcher William Tsuma (2010) describes community displacement as regular after the move to surface mining.
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: SGMC was dissolved by March 1997. Tarkwa output rose from 20,528 ounces (1989) to 47,450 ounces (1996). The World Bank rated the project highly satisfactory. The village of Abekoase reached an out-of-court settlement with the mining company in December 2003 (Earthworks).

sources.title: Ghana - Mining Sector Rehabilitation Project: Implementation Completion Report
Tarkwa, Ghana
Mining-Sector Reforms in Ghana: Institutionalizing and Legitimizing Large-Scale Land Deals

confidence_note: The World Bank documents its role in the sale. The 30,000 displacement figure covers all mines in the Wassa area, not only Tarkwa, and Earthworks does not name who counted it.

title: Hungary 1998 pension privatization

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Granted a one-tranche Public Sector Adjustment Loan (PSAL) of US$150 million. Its policy matrix, the conditions for Board presentation, included adopting a new mandatory private pension pillar and cutting public pension terms. An earlier US$132 million pension and health administration loan also supported the reform.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The ILO says the IMF and World Bank recommended pension privatization and soon dominated the reform debate.

conditions: PSAL policy actions: 'New multi-pillar system adopted', mandatory for new labour-force entrants; retirement age raised from 55 (women) and 60 (men) to 62; indexation changed from net wages to a mixed wage/price formula; private fund rules acceptable to the World Bank (World Bank IEG Hungary evaluation, 2007).
community: Pensions in the privatized system were estimated to be 9.8-12.5% lower than before for people with 20 years of contributions and over 18% lower with 30 years. Coverage fell from about 75% of the labour force (1998) to 71.8% (2009). Fund fees took 14.5% of contributions in 2007. Transition costs rose from 0.3% of GDP in 1998 to 1.2% in 2010 (ILO, 2018).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: Act CI of October 2010 moved private pension savings back to the state system. The government used 243 billion forints of the transferred assets to repay an IMF loan. The IMF, World Bank, EU and OECD criticized the reversal (ILO, 2018).

sources.title: Hungary - Pension reform and the development of pension systems: an evaluation of World Bank assistance
Reversing Pension Privatizations: Rebuilding public pension systems in Eastern Europe and Latin America
sources.publisher: International Labour Organization (Ortiz, Durán-Valverde, Urban, Wodsak, eds.)

confidence_note: Parliament passed the pension laws in 1996-1997; the World Bank evaluation says the PSAL conditions were to be met before the loan was granted.

title: Serbia 2015 state firm bankruptcies under IMF programme
point: Belgrade, seat of the Privatization Agency (firms were spread across Serbia)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Stand-By Arrangement approved 23 February 2015 (about €1.2 billion). In its policy memorandum the government committed to resolve over 500 firms by sale or bankruptcy, and ending state aid to the Železara Smederevo steelworks was a prior action.

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The government said it would start bankruptcies on the basis of an agreement with the World Bank (IMF Country Report 15/50).

conditions: Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies, para. 29: the government committed to resolve over 500 Privatization Agency firms 'through either privatization or bankruptcy'. An action plan for bankruptcy of 188 companies was adopted in early February 2015. Para. 30: eliminate all state aid to Železara Smederevo (prior action) (IMF Country Report 15/50).
community: Reuters reported about 5,000 job losses from the planned bankruptcy of the 188 firms. By mid-2016, about 300 firms employing about 25,000 workers had been liquidated, merged or sold. Five firms declared 'strategic', including Zastava vozila in Kragujevac, went bankrupt. The Heinrich Böll Foundation found no record of large severance payments in the budget.
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: About 250 firms with about 55,000 workers were still unresolved in July 2016, and 11 strategic firms with about 21,000 workers remained (Heinrich Böll Foundation).

sources.title: Republic of Serbia: 2014 Article IV Consultation and Request for Stand-By Arrangement (Country Report No. 15/50)
Serbia - Closing down of state-owned shell companies leads to 5,000 job losses
IMF Mission Has Left, Problems Remain

confidence_note: The government called the 188 firms loss-making shells. The 25,000 figure counts workers in firms resolved, not confirmed job losses.

title: Ukraine 2015 coal subsidy cut and miners' unpaid wages
point: Novovolynsk state coal mines, site of 2016 hunger strike (protests also in Kyiv)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Extended Fund Facility approved March 2015. The programme's 2015 budget eliminated subsidies to coal mining and cut subsidies to state firms by 1.1% of GDP. The Kyiv Post describes the cut as 'a stipulation' of the 2015 IMF loan.

conditions: Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies: the government 'eliminated price subsidies to the coal-mining industry' (worth 0.6% of GDP in 2014) as part of the 2015 budget (IMF Country Report 15/69).
community: On 28 January 2015 about 1,500 miners picketed the Cabinet of Ministers in Kyiv. Wage arrears stood at UAH 600 million (US$38 million), with some unpaid since August 2014. The union warned over 50,000 jobs were at risk (IndustriALL). In 2016 a state plan aimed to support only about a third of 35 state mines, close or sell the rest and cut about 10,000 jobs (20%). Miners were owed three months' pay (Kyiv Post).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: On 7 November 2016, 50 workers at the No. 10 Novovolynska mine began a hunger strike; earlier, 300 people from the mine blocked the Yahodyn checkpoint on the Polish border. The energy minister promised all wage debts would be paid by January 2017. The 2017 budget set coal support at UAH 1.8 billion, against the union's demand of UAH 4.6 billion.

sources.title: Ukraine: Request for Extended Arrangement under the Extended Fund Facility (Country Report No. 15/69)
State faces off with miners over subsidies to dying coal industry
Miners protest against destruction of coal mining in Ukraine

confidence_note: The war in eastern Ukraine also cut coal output and subsidies. The January 2015 protest came after the budget passed but before the IMF approved the new programme in March 2015.

title: Senegal 2023 fuel and electricity price rise
point: Dakar, capital (approximate); fare rises were also reported in Bignona

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Raising energy prices was a prior action (a step required before the IMF board meeting) in the January 2023 review of Senegal's Stand-By Arrangement, Standby Credit Facility and Policy Coordination Instrument (IMF Country Report 23/30).

conditions: IMF Country Report 23/30 lists as a prior action: 'Raise energy prices to limit electricity and fuel subsidies to 2.7 percent of GDP in 2023'. Publishing a roadmap to phase out energy subsidies by 2025 was also a prior action. Without action, subsidies were about 4.2% of GDP.
community: From January 2023 electricity rose by 18.97 CFA francs per kWh for low-voltage users and 22.79 for medium-voltage users, and diesel and premium fuel by 100 CFA francs per litre (Enerdata). Seneweb reported a shared-taxi ride in Bignona going from 500 to 1,000 CFA francs, and said bakers, carpenters, tailors and hairdressers faced higher power bills. The minibus operators' union Aftu announced fare rises.
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: The transport minister denied any agreed fare rise and said support for operators was being studied; a transport strike was called (Seneweb, 16 January 2023). The government expected to save about 258 billion CFA francs and aimed to end energy subsidies by 2025 (Enerdata). The IMF board completed the review in January 2023.

sources.title: Senegal: Sixth Review under the Policy Coordination Instrument and Third Reviews under the Stand-By Arrangement and the Standby Credit Facility (Country Report No. 23/30)

Senegal will remove energy sector subsidies by 2025

confidence_note: The IMF report gives no per-unit amounts; those come from Enerdata. The Bignona fare figure is a single local report.

title: Brazil 1999 IMF program social spending cuts
point: Brasília, where protesters gathered outside the World Bank office (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Three-year stand-by credit of SDR 13 billion (about US$18.1 billion) approved 2 December 1998, with primary surplus targets and spending cuts (IMF press release 98/59).

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Part of the financing package; in 1999 it also suspended loan disbursements to the states of Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul during their debt dispute with the federal government (Bretton Woods Project).

conditions: Primary surpluses of 2.6% of GDP in 1999, 2.8% in 2000 and 3% in 2001, with 'substantial cuts in discretionary current and capital spending', a higher financial transactions tax and higher pension contributions from public employees; budget savings of about 3.4% of GDP in 1999 (IMF press release 98/59).
community: Social Watch Brazil reports the social area lost R$2.04 billion (23.7%) in 1999 and 25 of 31 worker-funded programs for low-income people were ended. The Bretton Woods Project reports the 1999 land reform budget was cut 42.6% and sanitation 73%, and a rural settlements program was scrapped. Unemployment in Greater São Paulo reached 19.3% in 1999 (DIEESE/SEADE, cited by Social Watch).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: NGOs, unions, students and opposition parties protested outside the World Bank office in Brasília in early 1999. Brazil beat the IMF surplus target; Social Watch notes a R$30 billion primary surplus was absorbed by R$85 billion of federal debt interest (to September 1999).

sources.title: IMF Approves SDR 13 Billion Stand-By Credit for Brazil; Activates NAB (Press Release 98/59)
Brazilians protest spending cuts
Economic adjustment and social disadjustment

confidence_note: The IMF set overall surplus and cut targets; the choice of which programs to cut was the government's. Unemployment also reflects the January 1999 currency crisis.
